column2: I shall tell you this secret of dharma, best of the Bharatas, which Bhishma, or Yudhishthira the knower of dharma, would tell you,
or Vidura the minister, or the renowned Kunti; I shall tell you that in truth; understand it, Dhananjaya.
To speak the truth is good; there is nothing higher than truth; yet in its real nature it is very hard to know, for one who practises truth.
There are cases where truth should not be spoken and untruth should be spoken; when everything one owns is being taken, untruth should be spoken.
Untruth should be spoken when life is at stake and at a marriage; where untruth becomes truth and truth becomes untruth,
such is seen only by one who has truly practised truth; one who decides between truth and untruth becomes a knower of dharma.
What wonder if a man of resolved mind, even a very cruel one, obtained very great merit, like Balaka by killing the blind one?
What wonder again if a fool desiring dharma but unlearned incurred very great sin, like Kaushika at the river?
[Arjuna said:] "Tell me this, Lord, so that I may know the story linking Balaka and the blind one, and the rivers and Kaushika."
[Krishna said:] There was once a hunter of deer named Balaka, O Bharata, who killed deer not out of desire but for the livelihood of his wife and son.
He supported his blind mother and father and other dependants, ever devoted to his own duty, truthful in speech and free from envy.
Once, wishing for deer, he exerted himself but found none. Then he saw a beast that was drinking water, perceiving by smell and not by sight.
Though he had never seen such a creature, he killed it then; and immediately a shower of flowers fell from the sky.
A lovely celestial car, resounding with the songs and music of apsarases, came from heaven, wishing to take the hunter.
That creature, Arjuna, it is said, was made for the destruction of beings; having practised austerity it had obtained the boon of blindness, made by the Self-existent himself.
Having killed that being, resolved on the destruction of all beings, Balaka went to heaven. Thus dharma is very hard to know.
Kaushika too was a Brahmana, an ascetic, not much learned. He lived, it is said, at the confluence of rivers not far from a village.
I must always speak the truth—this was his vow, and he was renowned then as a truth-speaker, Dhananjaya.
Then some people, through fear of robbers, entered that forest, and the cruel robbers, going there, searched diligently.
Then they came to Kaushika and said to that truthful man: "By what path, Lord, did many people go? Asked, tell us truly, if you know."
Asked, Kaushika told them the truth: "They have taken refuge in this forest with many trees, creepers and thickets." Then those cruel men, reaching them, killed them, so it is heard.
By that great unrighteousness, through his ill-spoken word, Kaushika went to a very painful hell, unskilled in subtle dharmas, little learned, a fool, ignorant of the divisions of dharma.
Not having asked the elders about his doubt, he deserved a great pit. In this matter there may be some indication of the mark.
Supreme knowledge is hard; the doer decides here; many people say that dharma is what is heard (shruti).
I do not object to this, but not everything is laid down there; the teaching of dharma was made for the prosperity of beings.
They say dharma is that which sustains (dharana); dharma sustains the people; what is joined with sustaining is certainly dharma.
When some people wish to seize unjustly and release comes only by not speaking, one should not speak at all there.
Or if one must speak, or if silence would be suspected, it is considered better there to speak untruth than truth.
When life is at stake, at a marriage, when all kinsmen and wealth are being lost, or in jest, falsehood may be spoken; those who see the real meaning of dharma see no unrighteousness in it.
One who is freed from association with thieves even by oaths—it is better to speak untruth there; that is truth, without doubt.

And wealth should not be given to them in any way if it can be withheld; wealth should not be given to sinners if possible; therefore, having spoken untruth for dharma's sake, one does not become a speaker of untruth.
This indication of the mark has been stated to you duly. Having heard it, say, Partha, whether Yudhishthira deserves to be slain."
[Arjuna said:] "As the greatly wise, great-minded one would speak, and for our good, so this word of yours is.
You are to us like mother and like father, Krishna, and our supreme refuge; therefore your word is wondrous.
There is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you anywhere; therefore you know supreme dharma entirely as it is.
I regard the Pandava king of dharma, Yudhishthira, as not to be slain; in this joining of the pledge, say something gracious. And hear this other thing in my heart that I wish to say.
You know my vow, Dasharha: 'Whoever among men tells me, "Give Gandiva to another, Partha," or "He who is superior to you in weapons,"
I would slay him by force, Keshava; and Bhima would slay one called "tuvaraka" (beardless).' The king told me that in your presence, lion of the Vrishnis, repeatedly: 'Give up the bow.'

If, Keshava, I do not slay him in this living world, I cannot stand even a little while; and that vow of mine, known to the world, should be true, best of upholders of dharma. Give me such counsel today that the Pandava may live and I too, Krishna."
[Vasudeva said:] "The king is weary and wounded by Karna in battle with sharp masses of arrows; therefore, Partha, he spoke harsh words to you, for the gamble is staked today in battle on Karna.
If he is slain, the Kurus will be conquered; so thinks the king, son of Dharma. When one meets with great insult, then he is said to be dead while alive.
Therefore this king has always been honoured by you, Bhima and the twins, and by the elders and best of men in the world; so apply a small insult to him.
Say 'you' to him, Partha, to Yudhishthira; for an elder addressed as 'you' is as if slain, O Bharata.
Do so, son of Kunti, to the king of dharma Yudhishthira; make this unrighteous-seeming encounter, O Kuru bearer.
This is the Atharvangirasa, the highest of the revealed texts; those who desire welfare should always act on it without reflection.
For this is the 'slaying' of the king of dharma, Pandava, by you, and he will so understand it; then bow at his feet afterwards and speak of forgiveness, with soothing words, Partha.
Your wise brother, the Pandava king, will never be angry with you; freed from untruth and fratricide, Partha, glad, slay Karna the charioteer's son."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed by Janardana, Partha praised that "slaying of a friend," and then Arjuna said to the king of dharma a harsh word never said before, forcibly:

Do not speak, O king, among those who speak; you do not stand even a krosha from the half of the battle; Bhima deserves to blame me, who fights as the foremost hero among all warriors.

Through fear of dharma you would surely have undergone great austerity and a dreadful hell for killing your eldest brother.
So propitiate the king, best of upholders of dharma, righteous, best of the Kurus; this is my counsel here.

Having slain the very hard to conquer Karna today with sharp arrows, give great joy to the son of Dharma, giver of honour.
This, mighty-armed one, is in my view the right thing now; when it is done, your duty will have been done."
Then Arjuna, filled with shame, O great king, fell with his head at the feet of the king of dharma, sinless one.

Having wept for a long time, the two brothers of great splendour, tigers among men, purified themselves and became glad.

Today, having slain Karna, I shall come to you, O lord of the earth, to honour you, from that lament; this I tell you truly.
I shall not turn back from the battlefield today without slaying Karna; by this truth I touch your feet, lord of the earth."
[Sanjaya said:] Having propitiated the king of dharma, with a glad heart Partha said to Govinda, bent on the slaying of the charioteer's son:

Let the chariot be made ready again, and the best horses yoked, and let all weapons be arranged on the great chariot.
